claim: An increase in mechanical loading, such as that which occurs during resistance exercise, induces radial growth of muscle fibers (i.e. an increase in cross-sectional area).
source: An increase in mechanical loading, such as that which occurs during resistance exercise, induces radial growth of muscle fibers (i.e. an increase in cross-sectional area).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on resistance exercise and muscle fiber growth

claim: Muscle fibers are largely composed of myofibrils.
source: Muscle fibers are largely composed of myofibrils, but whether radial growth is mediated by an increase in the size of the myofibrils (i.e. myofibril hypertrophy) and/or the number of myofibrils (i.e. myofibrillogenesis) is not known.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about muscle fiber composition

claim: Whether radial growth is mediated by an increase in the size of the myofibrils (i.e. myofibril hypertrophy) and/or the number of myofibrils (i.e. myofibrillogenesis) is not known.
source: Muscle fibers are largely composed of myofibrils, but whether radial growth is mediated by an increase in the size of the myofibrils (i.e. myofibril hypertrophy) and/or the number of myofibrils (i.e. myofibrillogenesis) is not known.
evidence: Statement about the gap in knowledge that this study addresses

claim: FIM-ID is a novel method for visualizing myofibrils with a standard fluorescence microscope.
source: To overcome this, we developed a novel method for visualizing myofibrils with a standard fluorescence microscope (fluorescence imaging of myofibrils with image deconvolution [FIM-ID]).
evidence: Description of the method developed in this study

claim: Images from FIM-ID have a high degree of resolution and contrast.
source: Images from FIM-ID have a high degree of resolution and contrast, and these properties enabled us to develop pipelines for automated measurements of myofibril size and number.
evidence: Demonstrated through visual comparison in Figure 1 showing improved resolution after deconvolution

claim: FIM-ID enabled the development of pipelines for automated measurements of myofibril size and number.
source: Images from FIM-ID have a high degree of resolution and contrast, and these properties enabled us to develop pipelines for automated measurements of myofibril size and number.
evidence: Demonstrated through the validation studies in Figures 3 and 4

claim: The radial growth of muscle fibers is largely mediated by myofibrillogenesis in both mouse and human models of increased mechanical loading.
source: After extensively validating the automated measurements, we used both mouse and human models of increased mechanical loading to discover that the radial growth of muscle fibers is largely mediated by myofibrillogenesis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Figures 5 and 6 showing increased myofibril number

claim: Skeletal muscles comprise approximately 45% of the body's mass.
source: Comprising ~45% of the body's mass, skeletal muscles are not only the motors that drive locomotion, but they also play a critical role in respiration, whole-body metabolism, and maintaining a high quality of life (Izumiya et al., 2008; Srikanthan and Karlamangla, 2011; McLeod et al., 2016; Seguin and Nelson, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Skeletal muscles play a critical role in respiration, whole-body metabolism, and maintaining a high quality of life.
source: Comprising ~45% of the body's mass, skeletal muscles are not only the motors that drive locomotion, but they also play a critical role in respiration, whole-body metabolism, and maintaining a high quality of life (Izumiya et al., 2008; Srikanthan and Karlamangla, 2011; McLeod et al., 2016; Seguin and Nelson, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Both sedentary and active adults will lose 30–40% of their muscle mass by the age of 80.
source: Indeed, both sedentary and active adults will lose 30–40% of their muscle mass by the age of 80, and this loss in muscle mass is associated with disability, loss of independence, an increased risk of morbidity and mortality, as well as an estimated $40 billion in annual hospitalization costs in the United States alone (Seguin and Nelson, 2003; Janssen et al., 2004; Proctor et al., 1998; Pahor and Kritchevsky, 1998; Goates et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Loss of muscle mass is associated with disability, loss of independence, an increased risk of morbidity and mortality.
source: Indeed, both sedentary and active adults will lose 30–40% of their muscle mass by the age of 80, and this loss in muscle mass is associated with disability, loss of independence, an increased risk of morbidity and mortality, as well as an estimated $40 billion in annual hospitalization costs in the United States alone (Seguin and Nelson, 2003; Janssen et al., 2004; Proctor et al., 1998; Pahor and Kritchevsky, 1998; Goates et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Muscle mass loss is associated with an estimated $40 billion in annual hospitalization costs in the United States.
source: Indeed, both sedentary and active adults will lose 30–40% of their muscle mass by the age of 80, and this loss in muscle mass is associated with disability, loss of independence, an increased risk of morbidity and mortality, as well as an estimated $40 billion in annual hospitalization costs in the United States alone (Seguin and Nelson, 2003; Janssen et al., 2004; Proctor et al., 1998; Pahor and Kritchevsky, 1998; Goates et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Skeletal muscle mass can be regulated by mechanical signals.
source: Skeletal muscle mass can be regulated by a variety of different stimuli with one of the most widely recognized being mechanical signals (Bodine, 2013; Adams and Bamman, 2012; Goldberg et al., 1975; Roberts et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: An increase in mechanical loading can induce radial growth of the muscle fibers.
source: For instance, a plethora of studies have shown that an increase in mechanical loading, such as that which occurs during resistance exercise (RE), can induce radial growth of the muscle fibers (Conceição et al., 2018; Ema et al., 2016; Williams and Goldspink, 1971; Haun et al., 2019; Jorgenson et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: The ultrastructural adaptations that drive the radial growth response have not been well defined.
source: Surprisingly, however, the ultrastructural adaptations that drive this response have not been well defined (Haun et al., 2019; Jorgenson et al., 2020; Roberts et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature indicating gaps in knowledge

claim: Whether radial growth is mediated by an increase in the CSA of the individual myofibrils and/or the number of myofibrils has not been resolved.
source: For instance, during radial growth, the cross-sectional area (CSA) of the muscle fiber increases, but whether this is mediated by an increase in the CSA of the individual myofibrils (i.e. myofibril hypertrophy) and/or the number of myofibrils (i.e. myofibrillogenesis) has not been resolved (Jorgenson et al., 2020; Roberts et al., 2020; Wang et al., 1993; Ashmore and Summers, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature indicating gaps in knowledge

claim: A longstanding model in the field proposes that the radial growth of muscle fibers can be explained by a process called 'myofibril splitting'.
source: A longstanding model in the field proposes that the radial growth of muscle fibers can be explained by a process called 'myofibril splitting' (Goldspink, 1970; Goldspink, 1971; Patterson and Goldspink, 1976; Goldspink, 1983).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goldspink's work

claim: The myofibril splitting model was developed by Goldspink in the 1970s.
source: The myofibril splitting model was developed by Goldspink in the 1970s and contends that, during radial growth, myofibrils initially undergo hypertrophy.
evidence: Supported by citations to Goldspink's work

claim: According to the myofibril splitting model, during radial growth, myofibrils initially undergo hypertrophy.
source: The myofibril splitting model was developed by Goldspink in the 1970s and contends that, during radial growth, myofibrils initially undergo hypertrophy.
evidence: Description of Goldspink's model from cited literature

claim: According to the myofibril splitting model, as the CSA of the myofibrils increases, the outward radial force that they exert on the Z-disc increases.
source: Then, as the CSA of the myofibrils increases, the outward radial force that they exert on the Z-disc increases.
evidence: Description of Goldspink's model from cited literature

claim: According to the myofibril splitting model, when the outward radial forces reach a critical threshold the Z-disc will break.
source: The outward radial forces place a strain on the center of the Z-disc, and when the forces reach a critical threshold the Z-disc will break.
evidence: Description of Goldspink's model from cited literature

claim: According to the myofibril splitting model, the break will begin at the center of the Z-disc and form a longitudinal split that will propagate through the remainder of the myofibril.
source: It is proposed that the break will begin at the center of the Z-disc and form a longitudinal split that will then propagate through the remainder of the myofibril and, in turn, result in the formation of two smaller daughter myofibrils.
evidence: Description of Goldspink's model from cited literature

claim: Goldspink published images of single myofibrils that appeared to split into two smaller daughter myofibrils.
source: In support of his model, Goldspink published numerous images of single myofibrils that appeared to split into two smaller daughter myofibrils, as well as quantitative data which demonstrated that longitudinal splits usually occur in myofibrils that are significantly larger than myofibrils that do not contain splits (Goldspink, 1970; Goldspink, 1971; Patterson and Goldspink, 1976).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goldspink's work

claim: Goldspink published quantitative data demonstrating that longitudinal splits usually occur in myofibrils that are significantly larger than myofibrils that do not contain splits.
source: In support of his model, Goldspink published numerous images of single myofibrils that appeared to split into two smaller daughter myofibrils, as well as quantitative data which demonstrated that longitudinal splits usually occur in myofibrils that are significantly larger than myofibrils that do not contain splits (Goldspink, 1970; Goldspink, 1971; Patterson and Goldspink, 1976).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goldspink's work

claim: The myofibril splitting model has served as the textbook explanation of how muscle fibers undergo radial growth for decades.
source: This statement has been highlighted because, for decades, the myofibril splitting model has served as the textbook explanation of how muscle fibers undergo radial growth (MacIntosh and McComas, 2006; Komi, 2008; Bourne, 1972).
evidence: Supported by citations to textbooks

claim: The myofibril splitting model has not been rigorously tested.
source: However, after performing an exhaustive review of the literature, it was clear that this model has not been rigorously tested (Jorgenson et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review of the literature

claim: No study has shown that an increase in mechanical loading leads to an increase in the number of myofibrils per fiber.
source: For instance, in Goldspink's aforementioned conclusion, neither reference (Goldspink and Howells, 1974), nor any other study that we are aware of, has ever shown that an increase in mechanical loading leads to an increase in the number of myofibrils per fiber.
evidence: Based on review of literature and citation analysis

claim: Electron microscopy can provide images with the level of resolution needed to study myofibril structure.
source: When considering currently available technologies, electron microscopy (EM) would be viewed as the gold standard method for testing the myofibril splitting model; however, EM has several drawbacks/limitations.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about EM capabilities

claim: Electron microscopes are highly specialized instruments that require immense training and potentially cost-prohibitive user fees.
source: For instance, electron microscopes are highly specialized instruments, and their use requires immense training and potentially cost-prohibitive user fees.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about EM requirements

claim: The extensive fixation and processing required for EM often yields samples that are not readily amenable to immunolabeling.
source: Furthermore, the extensive fixation and processing required for EM often yields samples that are not readily amenable to immunolabeling (D'Amico et al., 2009), and EM images typically do not have a high degree of contrast between the area that is occupied by the myofibrils and the intermyofibrillar components that surround the myofibrils (e.g. the sarcoplasmic reticulum [SR], see Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: EM images typically do not have a high degree of contrast between the area occupied by myofibrils and the intermyofibrillar components.
source: Furthermore, the extensive fixation and processing required for EM often yields samples that are not readily amenable to immunolabeling (D'Amico et al., 2009), and EM images typically do not have a high degree of contrast between the area that is occupied by the myofibrils and the intermyofibrillar components that surround the myofibrils (e.g. the sarcoplasmic reticulum [SR], see Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by visual evidence in Figure 4A

claim: More than 180 myofibrils per fiber would have to be manually traced to estimate the mean myofibril CSA with a 5% margin of error at a 95% level of confidence.
source: We then used Cochran's formula to determine how many myofibrils per fiber would have to be measured to estimate the mean myofibril CSA with a 5% margin of error at a 95% level of confidence (Cochran, 1977). The outcomes revealed that >180 myofibrils per fiber would have to be manually traced.
evidence: Based on statistical calculation using Cochran's formula applied to pilot data

claim: A two-group comparison with 7 samples per group would require the manual tracing of more than 50,000 myofibrils.
source: Taking this a step further, it would mean that a two-group comparison with 7 samples per group would require the manual tracing of >50,000 myofibrils.
evidence: Based on calculation from the statistical requirements

claim: It took approximately 1 hour to manually measure 125 myofibrils.
source: In our hands, it took 1 hr to measure ≈125 myofibrils, and thus the simple two-group comparison described above would require ≈400 hr of manual tracing.
evidence: Based on empirical measurements of time required

claim: A simple two-group comparison would require approximately 400 hours of manual tracing.
source: In our hands, it took 1 hr to measure ≈125 myofibrils, and thus the simple two-group comparison described above would require ≈400 hr of manual tracing.
evidence: Based on calculation from empirical time measurements

claim: Myofibrils are largely surrounded by an SR that is highly enriched with SERCA.
source: To accomplish this, we took advantage of the fact that myofibrils are largely surrounded by an SR that is highly enriched with an enzyme called the sarco(endo)plasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase (SERCA) (Jorgensen et al., 1982; Rossi and Dirksen, 2006; Brandl et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: There are two major isoforms of SERCA: SERCA1 which is found in Type II fibers, and SERCA2 which is found in Type I fibers.
source: There are two major isoforms of SERCA (SERCA1 which is found in Type II fibers, and SERCA2 which is found in Type I fibers), and monoclonal antibodies for each isoform have been in existence for many years (Brandl et al., 1987; Braun et al., 2022; Johansson et al., 2003; Majerczak et al., 2008; Periasamy and Kalyanasundaram, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Monoclonal antibodies for SERCA1 and SERCA2 have been in existence for many years.
source: There are two major isoforms of SERCA (SERCA1 which is found in Type II fibers, and SERCA2 which is found in Type I fibers), and monoclonal antibodies for each isoform have been in existence for many years (Brandl et al., 1987; Braun et al., 2022; Johansson et al., 2003; Majerczak et al., 2008; Periasamy and Kalyanasundaram, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: SERCA antibodies have excellent reactivity in both flash-frozen and aldehyde-fixed tissues.
source: Importantly, these antibodies have been shown to possess excellent reactivity in both flash-frozen and aldehyde-fixed tissues (Nguyen et al., 2005; Rudolf et al., 2006; Toral-Ojeda et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Flash-frozen muscles can suffer from freezing artifacts that present as holes within the fibers.
source: This was not surprising because it is known that flash-frozen muscles can suffer from freezing artifacts that present as holes within the fibers (Meng et al., 2014; Nix and Moore, 2020; Gaspar et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Regions of poor myofibril integrity in flash-frozen samples were directly associated with the presence of freezing artifacts.
source: Thus, to determine if the integrity of the myofibrils was being distorted by freezing artifacts, we co-stained the cross-sections with phalloidin, and the results confirmed that regions of poor myofibril integrity were directly associated with the presence of freezing artifacts (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated through co-staining experiments shown in Figure 1B

claim: In 1973, Tokuyasu described a fixation and cryoprotection procedure that could preserve the ultrastructure of skeletal muscle at a level equivalent to that obtained with conventional resin-embedding procedures of EM.
source: In 1973, Tokuyasu described a fixation and cryoprotection procedure that could preserve the ultrastructure of skeletal muscle at a level that was equivalent to that obtained with the conventional resin-embedding procedures of EM (Tokuyasu, 1973).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tokuyasu's work

claim: Tissues preserved with the Tokuyasu method retain a high level of immunoreactivity and are amenable to immunolabeling.
source: Importantly, unlike resin-embedded tissues, it was shown that tissues preserved with the Tokuyasu method retain a high level of immunoreactivity and are therefore amenable to immunolabeling (Möbius and Posthuma, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: In 1982, the Tokuyasu method was used to define the ultrastructural localization of SERCA.
source: Indeed, in 1982, the Tokuyasu method was used to define the ultrastructural localization of SERCA (Jorgensen et al., 1982).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: The traditional Tokuyasu method requires sectioning temperatures that range from –50°C to –110°C.
source: However, the traditional Tokuyasu method requires sectioning temperatures that range from –50°C to –110°C, and such sectioning temperatures are dependent on the use of a cryo-ultramicrotome which is a rare and expensive instrument.
evidence: Based on description of the Tokuyasu method from cited literature

claim: SERCA immunoreactive cross-sections devoid of freeze artifacts could be obtained from muscles that had been extensively fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde and subsequently cryoprotected with 30–45% sucrose.
source: To examine the validity of our prediction we performed a lengthy series of trial-and-error experiments, and through these experiments, we discovered that SERCA immunoreactive cross-sections that were devoid of freeze artifacts could be obtained from muscles that had been extensively fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde and subsequently cryoprotected with 30–45% sucrose (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental optimization shown in Figure 1C-D

claim: The best integrity of the myofibrils was found in samples that had been cryoprotected with 45% sucrose.
source: Qualitatively, we concluded that the best integrity of the myofibrils was found in samples that had been cryoprotected with 45% sucrose and we also discovered that by lowering the sectioning temperature to –30°C we could eliminate sectioning artifacts that were readily present on the surface of samples that had been sectioned at warmer temperatures (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on qualitative assessment of experimental results shown in Figure 2

claim: Lowering the sectioning temperature to –30°C eliminated sectioning artifacts that were present at warmer temperatures.
source: Qualitatively, we concluded that the best integrity of the myofibrils was found in samples that had been cryoprotected with 45% sucrose and we also discovered that by lowering the sectioning temperature to –30°C we could eliminate sectioning artifacts that were readily present on the surface of samples that had been sectioned at warmer temperatures (Figure 2).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental comparison shown in Figure 2

claim: The resolution and contrast in widefield images can be negatively impacted by the acquisition of light that resides outside of the focal plane.
source: However, it is known that the resolution and contrast in widefield images can be negatively impacted by the acquisition of light that resides outside of the focal plane.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about widefield microscopy

claim: Major advancements in deconvolution algorithms have made it possible to reassign the out-of-focus light to its appropriate location.
source: Fortunately, major advancements in deconvolution algorithms have made it possible to reassign the out-of-focus light to its appropriate location (Stemmer et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: Deconvoluted widefield images can have better resolution and contrast than confocal images.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that deconvoluted widefield images can actually have better resolution and contrast than confocal images (Shaw, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: The application of the deconvolution algorithm led to a dramatic increase in the resolution and contrast of widefield images.
source: As shown in Figure 1E–F, the application of the deconvolution algorithm led to a dramatic increase in the resolution and contrast.
evidence: Demonstrated through visual comparison in Figure 1E-F

claim: There was a very high degree of agreement between the automated and manually obtained measurements of myofibril CSA.
source: As illustrated in Figure 3F, the comparisons revealed that there was a very high degree of agreement between the automated and manually obtained measurements of myofibril CSA.
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical comparison shown in Figure 3F

claim: A highly significant correlation (R=0.9589, p=0.0002) was observed when the automated measurements of myofibril CSA from each ROI were compared with the mean of the manual measurements.
source: Indeed, a highly significant correlation (R=0.9589, p=0.0002) was observed when the automated measurements of myofibril CSA from each ROI were compared with the mean of the manual measurements.
evidence: Statistical analysis of comparison data shown in Figure 3G

claim: All fibers in the plantaris muscles were SERCA1 positive.
source: With FIM-ID it was determined that all fibers in the plantaris muscles were SERCA1 positive, but during the EM imaging it became apparent that these SERCA1 positive fibers consisted of two clearly discernable fiber types.
evidence: Based on FIM-ID imaging results

claim: SERCA1 positive fibers in the plantaris consisted of two clearly discernable fiber types: glycolytic (Gly) and oxidative (Ox).
source: With FIM-ID it was determined that all fibers in the plantaris muscles were SERCA1 positive, but during the EM imaging it became apparent that these SERCA1 positive fibers consisted of two clearly discernable fiber types. One type was generally large in CSA and possessed very few intermyofibrillar mitochondria, and we referred to these fibers as glycolytic (Gly) (Figure 4A). The other type was generally small in CSA and highly enriched with intermyofibrillar mitochondria, and we referred to these fibers as oxidative (Ox) (Figure 4A).
evidence: Based on EM imaging observations shown in Figure 4A

claim: Myofibrils in fibers that are rich in mitochondria typically have a 'felderstruktur' appearance.
source: For instance, previous studies have shown that myofibrils in fibers that are rich in mitochondria typically have a 'felderstruktur' appearance (i.e. field structure) whereas myofibrils in fibers that lack extensive mitochondria present with a 'fibrillenstruktur' appearance (i.e. fibril structure) (Kruger and Gunther, 1955; Shear and Goldspink, 1971; Cheng and Breinin, 1965; Durston, 1974).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Myofibrils in fibers that lack extensive mitochondria present with a 'fibrillenstruktur' appearance.
source: For instance, previous studies have shown that myofibrils in fibers that are rich in mitochondria typically have a 'felderstruktur' appearance (i.e. field structure) whereas myofibrils in fibers that lack extensive mitochondria present with a 'fibrillenstruktur' appearance (i.e. fibril structure) (Kruger and Gunther, 1955; Shear and Goldspink, 1971; Cheng and Breinin, 1965; Durston, 1974).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: The FIM-ID- and EM-based measurements both revealed a linear correlation between myofibril CSA and fiber CSA.
source: As shown in Figure 4C, the FIM-ID- and EM-based measurements both revealed the linear correlation between myofibril CSA and fiber CSA that has been reported in previous studies (Jorgenson et al., 2020; Goldspink, 1970), and there was no significant difference in the slope of this correlation when the two methods were compared.
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical comparison shown in Figure 4C

claim: There was no significant difference in the slope of the correlation between myofibril CSA and fiber CSA when FIM-ID and EM methods were compared.
source: As shown in Figure 4C, the FIM-ID- and EM-based measurements both revealed the linear correlation between myofibril CSA and fiber CSA that has been reported in previous studies (Jorgenson et al., 2020; Goldspink, 1970), and there was no significant difference in the slope of this correlation when the two methods were compared.
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: No significant differences in mean myofibril CSA to fiber CSA ratio were found when the results from the FIM-ID and EM-based measurements were directly compared.
source: Moreover, no significant differences in mean myofibril CSA to fiber CSA ratio were found when the results from the FIM-ID and EM-based measurements were directly compared, and this point was true when the data from all analyzed fibers were considered, as well as when the results were separated according to the Ox and Gly fiber type (Figure 4E).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 4E

claim: The automated measurements of myofibril CSA obtained with FIM-ID were indistinguishable from the manually obtained EM-based measurements.
source: Thus, it can be concluded that the automated measurements of myofibril CSA obtained with FIM-ID were indistinguishable from the manually obtained EM-based measurements.
evidence: Based on statistical comparisons in Figures 4C and 4E

claim: The FIM-ID and EM-based measurements both revealed a linear correlation between myofibril number and fiber CSA.
source: As shown in Figure 4D, the FIM-ID and EM-based measurements both revealed the linear correlation between myofibril number and fiber CSA that has been reported in previous studies (Jorgenson et al., 2020; Goldspink, 1970), and there was no significant difference in the slope of this correlation when the two methods were compared.
evidence: Demonstrated through statistical comparison shown in Figure 4D

claim: There was no significant difference in the slope of the correlation between myofibril number and fiber CSA when FIM-ID and EM methods were compared.
source: As shown in Figure 4D, the FIM-ID and EM-based measurements both revealed the linear correlation between myofibril number and fiber CSA that has been reported in previous studies (Jorgenson et al., 2020; Goldspink, 1970), and there was no significant difference in the slope of this correlation when the two methods were compared.
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 4D

claim: No significant differences in the mean number of myofibrils per fiber CSA were found when the results from the FIM-ID and EM-based measurements were directly compared.
source: Moreover, no significant differences in the mean number of myofibrils per fiber CSA were found when the results from the FIM-ID and EM-based measurements were directly compared, and this point was true when the data from all analyzed fibers were considered, as well as when the results were separated according to the Ox and Gly fiber type (Figure 4F).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 4F

claim: The automated measurements of the number of myofibrils per fiber with FIM-ID were indistinguishable from the manually obtained EM-based measurements.
source: Hence, just like myofibril CSA, the automated measurements of the number of myofibrils per fiber with FIM-ID were indistinguishable from the manually obtained EM-based measurements.
evidence: Based on statistical comparisons in Figures 4D and 4F

claim: MOV led to a 28% increase in fiber CSA when all fibers in the muscle were considered as a single group.
source: As shown in Figure 5C, the outcomes revealed that MOV led to a 28% increase in fiber CSA when all fibers in the muscle were considered as a single group, and fiber type-specific analyses revealed that this was mediated by a 39% increase in the CSA of Ox fibers, and a 25% increase in the CSA of the Gly fibers.
evidence: Experimental data from MOV study shown in Figure 5C

claim: MOV led to a 39% increase in the CSA of Ox fibers.
source: As shown in Figure 5C, the outcomes revealed that MOV led to a 28% increase in fiber CSA when all fibers in the muscle were considered as a single group, and fiber type-specific analyses revealed that this was mediated by a 39% increase in the CSA of Ox fibers, and a 25% increase in the CSA of the Gly fibers.
evidence: Experimental data from MOV study shown in Figure 5C

claim: MOV led to a 25% increase in the CSA of Gly fibers.
source: As shown in Figure 5C, the outcomes revealed that MOV led to a 28% increase in fiber CSA when all fibers in the muscle were considered as a single group, and fiber type-specific analyses revealed that this was mediated by a 39% increase in the CSA of Ox fibers, and a 25% increase in the CSA of the Gly fibers.
evidence: Experimental data from MOV study shown in Figure 5C

claim: The area per fiber that was occupied by myofibrils increased by 29% for all fibers, 39% for the Ox, and 26% for the Gly in response to MOV.
source: Similarly, the area per fiber that was occupied by myofibrils increased by 29% for all fibers, 39% for the Ox, and 26% for the Gly (Figure 5D).
evidence: Experimental data from MOV study shown in Figure 5D

claim: The area per fiber that was occupied by the intermyofibrillar components showed a 26% increase for all fibers, a 38% increase in the Ox fibers, and a 22% increase in the Gly fibers in response to MOV.
source: Moreover, the area per fiber that was occupied by the intermyofibrillar components (e.g. SR, mitochondria, etc.) also showed a 26% increase for all fibers, a 38% increase in the Ox fibers, and a 22% increase in the Gly fibers.
evidence: Experimental data from MOV study shown in Figure 5E

claim: The MOV-induced increase in fiber CSA was mediated by a proportionate increase in the area that is occupied by the myofibrils and the area that is occupied by the intermyofibrillar components.
source: When taken together, these results indicate that the MOV-induced increase in fiber CSA was mediated by a proportionate increase in the area that is occupied by the myofibrils and the area that is occupied by the intermyofibrillar components.
evidence: Based on analysis of data in Figures 5C-E

claim: MOV increased the CSA of the individual myofibrils by 9% when all fibers were considered as a single group.
source: Specifically, we first examined whether MOV altered the CSA of the myofibrils and, as shown in Figure 5F, the outcomes revealed that MOV increased the CSA of the individual myofibrils by 9% when all fibers were considered as a single group, and fiber type-specific analyses revealed that MOV led to a 14% increase in the Ox fibers, but no significant difference was detected in the Gly fibers (p=0.35).
evidence: Experimental data from MOV study shown in Figure 5F

claim: MOV led to a 14% increase in myofibril CSA in the Ox fibers.
source: Specifically, we first examined whether MOV altered the CSA of the myofibrils and, as shown in Figure 5F, the outcomes revealed that MOV increased the CSA of the individual myofibrils by 9% when all fibers were considered as a single group, and fiber type-specific analyses revealed that MOV led to a 14% increase in the Ox fibers, but no significant difference was detected in the Gly fibers (p=0.35).
evidence: Experimental data from MOV study shown in Figure 5F

claim: No significant difference in myofibril CSA was detected in the Gly fibers in response to MOV (p=0.35).
source: Specifically, we first examined whether MOV altered the CSA of the myofibrils and, as shown in Figure 5F, the outcomes revealed that MOV increased the CSA of the individual myofibrils by 9% when all fibers were considered as a single group, and fiber type-specific analyses revealed that MOV led to a 14% increase in the Ox fibers, but no significant difference was detected in the Gly fibers (p=0.35).
